description: We are an ambitious engineering team bridging hardware design and modern software ecosystems. By combining AI generated physical device architectures with high performance mobile applications, we transform complex space challenges into tangible, scalable tech solutions. Building the smart tools for future space missions.
summary:
Orbital Medic is a health-monitoring system that lets astronauts assess their own health and act on it during long missions, without waiting for Earth. On the way to Mars a message to Mission Control can take up to 20 minutes one way, so the crew has to be its own first responder.

A screenless sensor band measures heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, skin temperature, the CO2 around the astronaut, radiation dose rate, motion, sleep and falls. The crew app (iPhone and web) adds a 2-minute daily check-in for blood pressure, blood sugar, mood, symptoms and vision. It compares every reading with safety limits and with the astronaut's own baseline, and shows the result as green, amber or red on an interactive body map, with plain step-by-step guidance tied to NASA Human Research Program risks.

Red alerts vibrate the band, alert crewmates, light the right compartment of the nearest emergency kit, and send an SOS automatically after a fall. A daily routine with XP and badges keeps up habits that prevent problems, such as exercise against bone loss. A flight surgeon console on Earth shows the whole crew, every value labeled with its age after the light-time delay.

This answers the challenge's key question: what the crew can handle on board right now, and when the ground needs to step in.
details:
What it does

Orbital Medic has four parts that share one assessment.

1. Orbital Medic Band: a screenless sensor band (ESP32-S3, MAX30102, MAX30205, Sensirion SCD41, MPU-6050, PIN-diode dosimeter, haptic motor, SOS button). It reads heart rate, HRV, SpO2, skin temperature, the CO2 the astronaut breathes, radiation dose rate, motion, sleep and falls, streams one frame per second over Bluetooth LE, and buzzes on its own even if the phone is off.

2. Crew app (native iPhone app in SwiftUI and a web app): live vitals, an interactive body map with seven tappable body systems, a 2-minute daily check-in (blood pressure, blood sugar, mood, symptoms, Amsler vision prompt), plain numbered guidance for every warning, a daily health routine with XP and badges, 30-day trend insights (sleep debt, mood decline, bone-loss estimate from NASA's 1-1.5% per month, mission radiation dose vs. a 600 mSv career limit), crewmate alerts, and an automatic SOS 15 seconds after an impact with no motion.

3. Emergency kit: a box with four lit compartments in each module, rover and airlock. The app lights the compartment that fits the alert (oxygen mask, glucose gel, auto-injector only after the Crew Medical Officer confirms, trauma kit). The kit never administers anything; a person decides. Demo builds use a needle-free trainer.

4. Flight surgeon console: the whole crew on one screen with KPIs, limit states, plots, 30-day trends, an alert timeline (detected on board, received on Earth, crew head start) and delayed uplink messages. Every value shows its age.

How it works

Every reading is checked against fixed safety limits and against the astronaut's own baseline (z-score), because "normal" shifts in microgravity. The result is nominal, caution or action required, and each indicator maps to one of NASA's five hazards (RIDGE) and a named HRP risk with a link to the source. The deep-space link is simulated with the real one-way light time (ISS, Moon 1.3 s, Mars 4-20 min); in the demo time is compressed 60x. Six emergency scenarios can be triggered: CO2 build-up, solar particle event, heart rhythm anomaly, cabin depressurization, fever and a fall.

Why it matters

On a Mars mission the crew cannot wait up to 40 minutes for an answer. Orbital Medic gives the astronaut an answer and an action in about one second, keeps flight surgeons informed with honest data-age labels, and builds daily habits that prevent problems.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks (hand-written SVG charts, Web Bluetooth, BroadcastChannel to simulate the space link); Swift and SwiftUI with Swift Charts and CoreBluetooth for the iPhone app; Arduino C++ for the ESP32 band and kit firmware. Wiring diagrams and parts lists are included (band about $25-90, kit about $16-22).

Limitations

Crew members and data are simulated unless a hardware band is connected. Limits are demonstration values; in a real mission a flight surgeon sets them. Orbital Medic is a prototype, not a medical device.

Team

Orbital Team: Oguz K. Gullu, Taha F. Kaya, Efe Pekuz, Mirac K. Kurtoglu, Dogukan Taplaktepe, Hanifi E. Korpe.
